results.summary: This project is titled test001 and is described only as a test Tiny Tapeout design. The documentation consists of placeholder text asking how the project works and how to test it, with no actual explanation. The pin names map the eight outputs to the segments and dot of a 7-segment display, but nothing states what is driven onto them. There is not enough information to determine the design's function or how it should be used.

This design implements four basic logic gates on a single tile: an AND of inputs 0 and 1, a NAND of inputs 2 and 3, an OR of inputs 4 and 5, and an XOR of inputs 6 and 7, with the results on outputs 0 through 3. It was created as an example for a Supercon workshop, presumably to teach the Tiny Tapeout design flow. Testing is done by driving the inputs and observing the gate outputs, and a silicon test report confirms each gate works as expected. No external hardware beyond the carrier board is described, and the documentation is otherwise minimal.

This project implements a low-baud-rate UART transmitter that repeatedly outputs the ASCII characters "Red." The inputs are labeled as bits 0 through 6, though the documentation does not explain how they configure the transmitter. Testing is done by connecting the TX and RX pins to a computer's serial port and observing the printed characters. The design is very small and its documentation is sparse, leaving the role of the input pins and the exact baud rate unclear.

The project is titled tt5modifyd and described only as a triple OR gate. The documentation contains placeholder text for how it works and how to test it, with no actual explanation of the inputs, outputs or behavior. The pin names map the outputs to 7-segment display segments, but nothing indicates what is displayed. There is not enough information to describe the design beyond its title.

This design demonstrates a hardware trojan based on a Medium article by Ryan Cornateanu, with two four-input circuits: a normal one on inputs 0-3 and a compromised one on inputs 4-7. The normal circuit's output appears on uo[0] and the trojan circuit's output on uo[6], so a user can compare behavior between the two. Testing uses DIP switches on the Tiny Tapeout carrier board, with no other external hardware required. It is intended as an educational illustration of how a hidden malicious circuit can differ from a trusted one.

This design implements a 4-bit LFSR configured as a PRBS generator with polynomial X^3+X^2+1, using XNOR feedback to avoid a synthesis warning. A clock input drives the shift register and a reset input clears the four flip-flops to zero so oscillation can start. The lower outputs drive a 7-segment display and the top output carries the PRBS stream. It was built as a simple design to verify the flow for teaching lower-division college students IC design, and testing consists of applying a clock and pulsing reset.

This design sends the string "Hello\n" over UART using a shift register with hardcoded initial values that is fed back into itself in an infinite loop. A load/enable input controls loading versus shifting, and an output enable gates the UART output, which appears on uo[7]. The remaining inputs and outputs are connected to a small flip-flop chain described jokingly as an RNN module that fills die space and is said to be trained on random Wokwi wiring. A silicon test report confirms that connecting the output to a serial port prints Hello.

This design is an 8-bit binary counter built from eight chained D flip-flops that increment on the clock input and present the count on the eight outputs. It deliberately lacks features such as a reset or a deterministic initial state, which the author notes as a limitation. It was constructed during the Hackaday Supercon 2023 ASIC workshop as a rapid learning exercise. Two silicon test reports confirm it counts correctly, with one noting roughly 20 Hz when clocked automatically.

The project is titled "IDK WHAT TO DO" and its one-line description is simply "Help me". The documentation contains only the default placeholder prompts for how the project works and how to test it. The pin names map the outputs to 7-segment display segments, but no function is described. There is essentially no information about what the design does or how it should be used.
